stem: What are the products when ethanol burns completely in air?

options.rationale: These are the products of dehydration, not combustion.
C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O.
Ethanoic acid forms when ethanol is oxidised gently, not burnt.
Complete combustion gives fully oxidised products: CO₂ and H₂O.

explanation: Ethanol burns completely to carbon dioxide and water, releasing heat: C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O.

stem: Which are two important uses of ethanol?

options.content: as a fuel and as a solvent
options.rationale: Ethanol burns cleanly and dissolves many substances.

options.content: as a fertiliser and as an explosive
options.rationale: Ethanol is used for neither.

options.content: as a bleach and as a water softener
options.rationale: Ethanol is used for neither.

options.content: as a catalyst and as a refrigerant gas
options.rationale: Ethanol is a liquid at room temperature and is not a catalyst.

explanation: Ethanol is used as a fuel (burns releasing heat with little soot) and as a solvent (for perfumes, inks, varnishes and medicines).

stem: Which is the balanced equation for the complete combustion of ethanol?

options.rationale: Oxygen: 5 on the left but 7 on the right.
Hydrogen: 6 on the left but 4 on the right.
Neither carbon (2 and 1) nor hydrogen (6 and 2) is balanced.

explanation: Ethanol contains 2 C, 6 H and 1 O. Two CO₂ and three H₂O contain 7 O atoms, so 6 O atoms (3O₂) must come from oxygen: C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O.

stem:
True or false: ethanol mixes completely with water in all proportions.

*Syllabus note: ZIMSEC O-Level Form 4 content.*

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Correct: the –OH group lets ethanol mix with water in any amount.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: It is true. Ethanol is completely miscible with water; that is why alcoholic drinks are a single liquid layer.

explanation: The –OH group of ethanol is attracted to water molecules, so ethanol and water mix in all proportions to form one layer.

stem:
Ethanol is warmed with acidified potassium dichromate(VI). State the colour change seen.

*Syllabus note: ZIMSEC O-Level Form 4 content.*

patterns: ^(.* )?(from )?orange ?(to|into|→|>|then|becomes|turns|turned|turns to|changes to|changed to|goes to|turned to)( a)?( dark| blue| pale)? ?green( colou?r| solution)?$

rejected.feedback: The dichromate starts orange and turns green.
The dichromate starts orange and turns green.
That is the change for acidified potassium manganate(VII).

explanation: Acidified potassium dichromate(VI) is orange. It oxidises ethanol to ethanoic acid and is itself reduced, turning green. This is the test for ethanol.

wrongResponses.text: it changes from green to orange
it stays orange and does not turn green

stem:
What is formed when ethanol is warmed with acidified potassium dichromate(VI)?

*Syllabus note: ZIMSEC O-Level Form 4 content.*

options.rationale: Ethanol is oxidised: CH₃CH₂OH → CH₃COOH.
Ethene forms when ethanol is dehydrated, not oxidised.
Ethane would need hydrogen to be added, not oxygen.
This ester forms when ethanol reacts with ethanoic acid.

explanation: Acidified potassium dichromate(VI) is an oxidising agent. It oxidises ethanol to ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH, and turns from orange to green.
hints: Dichromate is an oxidising agent: what does ethanol become when it is oxidised?

stem:
Which conditions convert ethanol into ethene, and what type of reaction is this?

*Syllabus note: ZIMSEC O-Level Form 4 content.*

options.content: warming with acidified potassium dichromate(VI); oxidation
options.rationale: This gives ethanoic acid, not ethene.
Fermentation makes ethanol from sugar.

options.content: heating with hydrogen and nickel; hydrogenation
options.rationale: Hydrogenation adds hydrogen to alkenes.

options.content: passing ethanol vapour over hot aluminium oxide; dehydration
options.rationale: A molecule of water is removed: C₂H₅OH → C₂H₄ + H₂O.

explanation: Hot aluminium oxide (or excess concentrated sulfuric acid) removes water from ethanol: C₂H₅OH → C₂H₄ + H₂O. Removing water is called dehydration.
hints: Compare the formulae C₂H₅OH and C₂H₄: what has been removed?

stem:
Calculate the mass of water produced when 11.5 g of ethanol burns completely. $\ce{C2H5OH + 3O2 -> 2CO2 + 3H2O}$ (Aᵣ: H = 1, C = 12, O = 16)

*Syllabus note: calculations with moles and gas volumes are Cambridge IGCSE Supplement (Extended) content.*
explanation: n(ethanol) = 11.5 ÷ 46 = 0.25 mol. Each mole gives 3 mol of water: 0.75 mol × 18 = 13.5 g.
hints: Use the 1 : 3 ratio of ethanol to water.

stem:
What volume of oxygen, measured at room temperature and pressure, is needed to burn 4.6 g of ethanol completely? (Mᵣ of ethanol = 46; one mole of gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p.)

*Syllabus note: calculations with moles and gas volumes are Cambridge IGCSE Supplement (Extended) content.*
explanation: n(ethanol) = 4.6 ÷ 46 = 0.10 mol. C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O, so 0.30 mol of O₂ is needed: 0.30 × 24 = 7.2 dm³.
hints: Write the balanced equation first: 1 mol of ethanol needs 3 mol of oxygen.

stem:
Complete the description of ethanol.

*Syllabus note: ZIMSEC O-Level Form 4 content.*

payload.template: Ethanol is a {{blank:a}} liquid that boils at {{blank:b}} °C. It {{blank:c}} with water.

explanation: Ethanol is a colourless liquid, boiling point 78 °C (it freezes at −114 °C), which mixes completely with water.

stem:
Match each use of ethanol with the property that makes it suitable.

*Syllabus note: ZIMSEC O-Level Form 4 content.*

left.content: liquid in thermometers for very cold places

right.content: burns readily, releasing a lot of heat with little soot
dissolves fragrant oils and evaporates quickly from the skin
kills many bacteria and viruses on the skin

explanation: Each use depends on a property: combustion (fuel), solvent power and volatility (perfume), antiseptic action (sanitiser) and a very low freezing point (thermometers). Ethanol is neutral, so it does not neutralise acids.
hints: Ethanol is neutral: it is not a base.

stem:
Three unlabelled bottles, P, Q and R, contain water, ethanol and hexane (in some order). Nyasha carries out three tests.

| Test | P | Q | R |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| mixed with an equal volume of water | one layer | two layers | one layer |
| a few drops lit on a watch glass | does not burn | burns with a smoky yellow flame | burns with a pale blue flame |
| warmed with acidified potassium dichromate(VI) | stays orange | stays orange | turns green |

*Syllabus note: ZIMSEC O-Level Form 4 content.*

options.rationale: P does not burn: it is water.
Q forms a separate layer and burns with a smoky flame: it is hexane.
Burns with a clean flame, mixes with water and turns dichromate green.

options.content: It cannot be decided from these results.
options.rationale: The dichromate test alone identifies R as ethanol.
P does not burn, so it is water.
It does not mix with water and burns with a smoky flame.
R turns dichromate green, so it is ethanol.
Only one bottle contains hexane.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why hexane forms a separate layer with water but ethanol does not.

points.description: Ethanol has an –OH group that is attracted to water molecules; hexane is a hydrocarbon with no –OH group, so it does not mix with water

parts.explanation: Ethanol's –OH group is attracted to water molecules, so it mixes completely; hexane is a hydrocarbon with no –OH group, so it does not mix and floats as a separate layer.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Name the organic product formed in the dichromate test with R.

rejected.feedback: Dichromate oxidises ethanol to ethanoic acid; ethene is made by dehydration.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Suggest **one** safety precaution Nyasha should take when burning the liquids.

points.description: Use only a few drops / keep the bottles of ethanol and hexane away from the flame / wear eye protection / work on a heat-proof mat

parts.explanation: Burn only a few drops on a watch glass on a heat-proof mat, and keep the stock bottles of the flammable liquids well away from any flame.

explanation: P is water (does not burn), Q is hexane (immiscible with water, smoky flame, no reaction with dichromate) and R is ethanol (miscible, clean blue flame, turns acidified dichromate green as it is oxidised to ethanoic acid).
workedSolution:
1. Does not burn → water (P).
2. Two layers + sooty flame + no dichromate change → hexane (Q).
3. Turns dichromate green → ethanol (R), oxidised to ethanoic acid.
hints: Which liquid does not burn at all?

stem:
Ethanol vapour is passed over heated aluminium oxide. A colourless gas is collected over water.

*Syllabus note: ZIMSEC O-Level Form 4 content.*

rejected.feedback: Removing water from ethanol gives the alkene ethene, not ethane.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: What type of reaction is this?

options.rationale: Water is removed from the ethanol molecule.
Hydration adds water; it is the reverse reaction.
Oxidation of ethanol gives ethanoic acid.
Fermentation makes ethanol from sugar.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Which test confirms that the gas is unsaturated?

options.rationale: That is the test for carbon dioxide.

options.content: A lighted splint gives a squeaky pop.
options.rationale: That is the test for hydrogen.

options.content: Acidified potassium dichromate(VI) turns from orange to green.
options.rationale: That is the test for ethanol.

options.content: Bromine water turns from orange to colourless.
options.rationale: Ethene adds bromine across its C=C bond.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Explain why the delivery tube must be removed from the water before the heating is stopped.

points.description: To prevent suck-back: as the tube cools, cold water would be drawn back into the hot tube and crack it

parts.explanation: When heating stops, the gas in the tube contracts and cold water would be sucked back into the hot glass, which could crack it.

explanation: Hot aluminium oxide dehydrates ethanol: C₂H₅OH → C₂H₄ + H₂O. Ethene is unsaturated, so it decolourises bromine water. Removing the delivery tube first prevents suck-back.
workedSolution:
1. (a) Ethene.
2. (b) H₂O.
3. (c) Dehydration.
4. (d) Bromine water orange → colourless.
5. (e) Prevent suck-back.

stem:
Describe **four** social effects of the misuse of alcohol (ethanol) in a community. [4]

*Syllabus note: ZIMSEC O-Level Form 4 content.*

points.description: Health: addiction (alcoholism), liver damage (cirrhosis), damage to the brain or heart
Road accidents caused by drunk driving; injuries
Violence and crime, including domestic violence; family breakdown
Money spent on alcohol instead of food or school fees; poverty
Absenteeism and loss of jobs / lower productivity
Risky behaviour such as unprotected sex, increasing the spread of HIV
Illegal brews containing methanol can cause blindness or death

answerSpec.modelAnswer: People who misuse alcohol can become addicted and suffer liver damage. Drunk drivers cause road accidents in which people are injured or killed. Alcohol misuse is linked to violence, including domestic violence, and to family breakdown. Money is spent on alcohol instead of food and school fees, and drinkers may miss work and lose their jobs. Drunkenness also lowers judgement, leading to unprotected sex and a greater risk of HIV infection.

explanation: Each specific effect (health, accidents, violence, money and jobs, risky behaviour, methanol poisoning) earns a mark; vague statements such as 'alcohol is bad' do not.
hints: Think of effects on health, on safety, on families and on money.

stem: Which property makes ethanol suitable for use as a **fuel**?

options.rationale: Mixing with water does not make a substance burn well.

options.content: It burns readily, releasing a lot of heat with little soot.
options.rationale: This is what a good fuel does.

options.content: It is a good solvent for oils.
options.rationale: This makes it useful as a solvent, not as a fuel.

options.content: It turns acidified potassium dichromate(VI) from orange to green.
options.rationale: This is a test for ethanol, not a reason to burn it.

explanation: A fuel must burn easily and release a lot of energy. Ethanol burns readily with a clean flame (complete combustion to CO₂ and H₂O), so it is used in spirit burners and fuel blends.

stem:
True or false: methylated spirits is safe to drink because it is mostly ethanol.

*Syllabus note: ZIMSEC O-Level Form 4 content.*

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: It is false. Methylated spirits contains methanol, which is poisonous and can cause blindness or death.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: Correct: methylated spirits contains poisonous methanol and must never be drunk.

explanation: Methylated spirits is ethanol to which methanol (and other substances) has been added to make it undrinkable. Methanol is poisonous: small amounts can cause blindness or death.

stem:
Ethanol (Mᵣ 46) boils at 78 °C, but butane (Mᵣ 58) boils at −1 °C, even though butane molecules are heavier. Which is the best explanation?

*Syllabus note: ZIMSEC O-Level Form 4 content.*

options.content: Ethanol molecules contain more atoms, so the forces between them are stronger.
options.rationale: Ethanol (C₂H₆O) has 9 atoms and butane (C₄H₁₀) has 14; size is not the reason.

options.content: Ethanol is an ionic compound, so it has strong forces between its ions.
options.rationale: Ethanol is a covalent molecule; it contains no ions.

options.content: The –OH group makes the forces between ethanol molecules much stronger.
options.rationale: Stronger intermolecular forces need more energy to overcome.

options.content: The covalent bonds inside butane molecules are weaker, so they break more easily.
options.rationale: Boiling separates molecules; it does not break the covalent bonds inside them.

explanation: Boiling overcomes the forces between molecules. Ethanol's –OH group makes these forces much stronger than those between butane molecules, so ethanol has a much higher boiling point even though its molecules are lighter.
hints: What does boiling separate: atoms or molecules?
Mass alone cannot explain it: butane is the heavier molecule.

stem: A spirit burner containing ethanol is used to heat a beaker of water. During the experiment the mass of the burner falls by 2.3 g. (Aᵣ: H = 1, C = 12, O = 16)

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Balance the equation for the complete combustion of ethanol.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem:
Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide produced.

*Syllabus note: calculations with moles and gas volumes are Cambridge IGCSE Supplement (Extended) content.*

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Soot appears on the bottom of the beaker. Name the poisonous gas that may also form.

rejected.feedback: Carbon dioxide forms in complete combustion; incomplete combustion can form carbon monoxide.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Ethanol made from sugar cane is described as a **renewable** fuel. Explain why.

points.description: It is made from a crop (sugar cane) that can be grown again each season, so it will not run out

parts.explanation: It is made by fermenting sugar from sugar cane, which can be replanted and harvested again, so the supply will not run out.

explanation: C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O. n(ethanol) = 2.3 ÷ 46 = 0.050 mol, giving 0.10 mol CO₂ = 4.4 g. Soot shows incomplete combustion, which can also form carbon monoxide. Ethanol from sugar cane is renewable because the crop can be grown again.
workedSolution:
1. (a) 2 C → 2CO₂; O: 4 + 3 = 7, minus 1 in ethanol = 6 → 3O₂.
2. (b) n = 2.3 ÷ 46 = 0.050 mol; n(CO₂) = 0.10 mol; mass = 0.10 × 44 = 4.4 g.
3. (c) Carbon monoxide.
4. (d) Made from a crop that can be regrown.
hints: Remember the oxygen atom already in the ethanol molecule.

stem:
An early type of breathalyser contained orange crystals of acidified potassium dichromate(VI) in a glass tube. A driver blew through the tube, and any ethanol vapour in the breath turned some of the crystals green. The further along the tube the green colour reached, the more alcohol there was in the breath.

*Syllabus note: ZIMSEC O-Level Form 4 content.*

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: What happens to the ethanol in the tube?

options.rationale: Dehydration needs hot aluminium oxide or concentrated sulfuric acid.
Dichromate(VI) is an oxidising agent.
Fermentation makes ethanol; it does not remove it.
No hydrogen is involved.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why the length of the green section indicates how much alcohol was in the breath.

points.description: Each portion of dichromate can react with only a limited amount of ethanol
More ethanol reacts with (and turns green) more of the crystals, so the green colour spreads further along the tube

parts.explanation: Each crystal can oxidise only a fixed amount of ethanol. Breath containing more ethanol needs more crystals to react with it, so the green colour spreads further along the tube.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Suggest why this test does not prove that the substance in the breath was ethanol.

points.description: Other substances that can be oxidised (such as other alcohols, e.g. methanol or propan-1-ol) also turn dichromate green

parts.explanation: Other alcohols, such as methanol or propan-1-ol, are oxidised in the same way and also turn the dichromate green, so the test is not specific to ethanol.

explanation: Acidified dichromate(VI) oxidises ethanol to ethanoic acid and changes from orange to green. The amount turned green depends on the amount of ethanol. Other oxidisable substances, such as other alcohols, give the same colour change.
workedSolution:
1. (a) Oxidation.
2. (b) Ethanoic acid.
3. (c) Fixed amount per crystal → more ethanol, longer green section.
4. (d) Other alcohols also reduce dichromate.

stem: Why is ethanol used as the solvent in perfumes?

options.content: It reacts with the fragrant oils to make new, longer-lasting smells.
options.rationale: A solvent dissolves substances without reacting with them.

options.content: It forms an oily layer on the skin that traps the scent for hours.
options.rationale: Ethanol evaporates within seconds; it does not form an oily layer.

options.content: It dissolves the fragrant oils and evaporates quickly from warm skin.
options.rationale: The scent is carried into the air as the ethanol evaporates.

options.content: It hardly evaporates, so the scent stays on the skin all day.
options.rationale: Ethanol evaporates easily (boiling point 78 °C).

explanation: Ethanol dissolves the oils that give perfumes their scent (water cannot), and it evaporates quickly from warm skin, carrying the scent with it.
